turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, doctor, it's just... I can't seem to keep my mind on one thing anymore, and it's really starting to become a problem. I mean, I've been a carpenter for a long time, and you need to be able to focus, you know? But lately, it's like every little thing pulls me away. Just the other day, I was measuring out some baseboards for a client's living room, and I heard a saw starting up a few houses down—someone doing their own renovations, I guess—and immediately, my brain is just gone. I start wondering what kind of saw it is, what they're building, if they know what they're doing... and before I know it, I've completely lost my place. Or if I'm in the office doing paperwork, which is hard enough for me anyway, somebody walking past the window is enough to make me stop and stare. Even my own thoughts are a problem! I'll be right in the middle of sanding a cabinet, and a thought about another job across town will pop into my head, and suddenly I'm trying to figure out the materials list for *that* job instead of finishing the one right in front of me. And then, you know what happens? The whole day just gets away from me. I look at my watch, and it's 4:00 PM, and I've got half-finished projects everywhere and nothing actually done. It's exhausting, honestly, just trying to keep my brain in one place.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient reports an inability to keep their mind on one thing and difficulty focusing on tasks like measuring baseboards or sanding cabinets.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient states they end the workday with 'half-finished projects everywhere and nothing actually done,' indicating a failure to finish workplace duties.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (a saw starting up, someone walking past a window) as well as unrelated thoughts (thinking about another job).

turns.doctor_question: Looking back to your childhood or school years, did you experience similar difficulties with focus and attention?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, yes. Yes, I definitely did. You know, it's funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my sister about this the other day. We were going through some old boxes of our mother's things—she passed away a few years ago—and we found a stack of my old report cards from elementary school. I mean, way back, like second, third, fourth grade. And reading through the comments... well, it was like reading about the exact same person sitting in front of you today. 

Every single year, it was the same story. The teachers would always write things like, "She's a very bright girl, but she's so careless," or "She needs to apply herself." I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was this very strict, older woman with these glasses on a chain—she called my mother in for a conference because I was constantly losing my homework. I would do it, I swear I would do it, sitting at the kitchen table, but then between the table and my backpack, or my backpack and my desk at school, it would just vanish. Poof. Gone. 

And instructions? Forget about it. The teacher would stand at the front of the room and say, "Okay, class, take out your math book, turn to page forty-two, and do the even numbers." And by the time I opened my desk to get the book, I was already thinking about what we were going to play at recess, or watching a bird outside the window. I spent *so* much time staring out the window. I'd be looking at the clouds, or the janitor mowing the lawn, or literally anything besides the worksheet on my desk. 

My mother used to get so frustrated with me. She'd say, "You're smart enough to do this, why won't you just focus?" But I couldn't explain it to her then, and I guess I still can't explain it now. It wasn't that I didn't want to do the work, it was just... my brain would just drift away. So, yes, definitely before I was twelve, this was already a huge issue. It's just that back then, they just called it daydreaming or being careless, you know? They didn't really have a name for it. But it's always been there, just this constant struggle to keep my head in the game.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that teachers frequently noted she was 'careless' in her schoolwork.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a 'constant struggle to keep my head in the game' and that her brain would 'drift away' during tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states she had trouble following through on instructions, forgetting them before she could even start the task.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions constantly losing her homework between doing it and turning it in.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as birds, clouds, or the janitor outside the window.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel physically restless, like you have trouble sitting still or feel an inner drive to constantly be on the go?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's not so much that I'm bouncing off the walls or running around like a motor, but... yes, definitely. It's more of an inside feeling, if that makes sense? Like this tight, wound-up sensation right in my chest or my stomach. It happens the most when I'm stuck doing the paperwork side of things. If I have to sit at the desk in my office—which is really just a corner of the garage that I tried to make look professional—and do estimates or go through invoices, I just... I can't stand it. 

I'll be sitting there, and I know I need to finish, especially right now because I actually broke my wrist a while back and it's finally healed up, so I really should just be catching up on all the admin stuff I put off. I know I'm supposed to just stay put and get it done. But after about ten minutes, my legs start feeling twitchy, and I get this overwhelming urge to just stand up and do *something* else. Anything else. I'll get up to get a glass of water, or I'll suddenly decide I need to reorganize my drill bits, or I'll just pace around the driveway for a few minutes. 

And if I'm stuck in a long meeting—like when I have to sit down with a general contractor and go over blueprints for an hour—it takes every ounce of my willpower just to stay in the chair. I'll be shifting my weight, tapping my foot, playing with a pen, just feeling this intense pressure inside like I need to get up and move around right that second. It's exhausting, honestly, trying to force myself to stay still when my whole body is screaming at me to get up and go do something physical. It's like my brain and my body are just totally out of sync when I have to sit still.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient reports shifting their weight, tapping their foot, and playing with a pen when forced to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes getting up to get water or pace around when they know they are expected to stay seated and finish their work.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms feeling a tight, wound-up sensation and an intense inner pressure to get up and move around.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies bouncing off the walls or acting as if driven by a motor.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself blurting out answers before someone finishes asking, or having a hard time waiting for your turn in conversations?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I don't think I do that. It's funny, because my brother—he's a plumber, actually, works out in the suburbs mostly—he's terrible about that. You can't get a word in edgewise with him, he's always jumping in and finishing your sentences. But for me... no, I don't have that problem. 

Actually, if anything, I'm usually the one who's quiet in a group conversation. Not because I don't have anything to say, mind you, but because by the time I've figured out what they're talking about, or I've stopped thinking about the grocery list or whatever else popped into my head, the conversation has already moved on to three different topics. Like, the other day I was at the lumber yard, talking to the guys behind the counter—Frank and Joe, I've known them for fifteen years, since I first started out on my own—and they were talking about this new zoning law the city is trying to pass. And I wanted to say something about how it's going to affect the permit process for the kind of deck additions I usually build, but I got distracted trying to remember if I had enough galvanized screws in the truck. By the time I tuned back in, they were talking about the baseball game from the night before. So, I just sort of nodded along. 

So, yeah, I don't really blurt things out or interrupt people. I'm usually too busy being lost in my own head to even realize it's my turn to talk, let alone jump the gun on it. I just kind of sit there and try to piece together what I missed while my brain was taking a little vacation.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes getting distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as grocery lists or work supplies, during conversations.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies blurting things out.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient denies having a hard time waiting for their turn in conversations.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly states they do not interrupt people.
